title: Dual Coding in Action: The Power of Sketch and Tell
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A classroom teacher explains Paivio's dual coding theory and offers a simple routine, Sketch and Tell, for applying it. Students draw a representation of a concept and then explain it in words, with the two saying the same thing in different ways. The author runs it on mini whiteboards, follows with a Think-Pair-Share for extra retrieval and rehearsal, and teaches students the science behind the routine so it is not seen as doodling. The piece lists variations across vocabulary, processes, cause and effect, comparisons, timelines, and analogies. Its central claim is that dual coding is about deeper processing and two memory traces, not pretty pictures.
points: Encoding information in both verbal and visual channels creates multiple retrieval pathways and more durable memory.
Sketch and Tell is a low-prep routine: draw, then explain, with stick figures acceptable because the goal is meaning-making.
Adding mini whiteboards and Think-Pair-Share lets the teacher see thinking in real time while adding retrieval and rehearsal.
Telling students why the routine works gives them a rationale and makes them active participants in building memory.
The strategy adapts to many content types, from vocabulary and processes to timelines, analogies, and prediction sketches.
quotes: When information is encoded in both channels, learners create two mental representations of the same knowledge. That means when students later try to retrieve it, they have multiple pathways back to the memory.
What makes dual coding especially powerful is the way the two systems reinforce each other. Words can clarify visuals, and visuals can anchor abstract words.

I always tell students that the “sketch” and the “tell” should say the same thing but in different ways. The drawing doesn’t need to be artistic either; stick figures and symbols work just fine. The goal is meaning-making, not art.
I often have students do this on mini whiteboards, which lets me quickly see their thinking in real time. Once they’ve sketched and written, I’ll turn it into a quick Think-Pair-Share.

They know it isn’t busywork or just a chance to doodle mindlessly, it’s a proven way to make knowledge easier to retrieve later. Framing it this way gives students a clear why behind the routine and helps them see themselves as active participants in building long-term, accessible memory.
Dual coding isn’t about pretty pictures; it’s about deeper processing. Sketch and Tell helps students slow down, visualize, and explain which strengthens their memory and makes learning stick.
